artworks.title: 'Au clair de la lune' phonautogram

date.label: 9 April 1860 (date written on the phonautogram sheet)

location.name: Paris
location.institution: Académie des sciences (the 1860 phonautogram sheets, deposited by Scott in 1861)

artworks.medium: Phonautogram: sound-wave trace scratched by a stylus into lampblack on paper; recovered as audio in 2008
artworks.description: Seventeen years before Edison's phonograph, a Parisian typesetter and amateur scientist, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, built a machine that wrote sound down. His phonautograph gathered sound in a horn, let it shake a membrane, and had a hog's bristle scratch the vibration into lampblack on paper turning on a cylinder. Scott wanted a way to read speech from the squiggle; he never imagined playing it back. On 9 April 1860 he sang a few seconds of the folk song 'Au clair de la lune' into the horn and dated the sheet. In 2008 the First Sounds group had the trace scanned at high resolution and turned back into sound by computer at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the thin, wavering voice that emerged is the oldest recording of a human voice that can be recognised. The drawing shown is Scott's own sketch of his machine from his 1859 patent papers. The visitor hears the eleven-second 2008 recovery.
facts: The sheet was deposited with the Académie des sciences in Paris in 1861 and lay unplayed for 147 years.
The first 2008 playback ran at the wrong speed and was taken for a girl's voice; correcting the cylinder speed revealed a slow male voice, probably Scott's own.
Scott patented the phonautograph on 25 March 1857; Edison's phonograph, the first machine that could play sound back, followed in 1877.

artworks.title: Luncheon on the Grass
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
subjects: still life of fruit and bread
artworks.description: Two young men in the clothes of 1863 sit on the grass with a naked woman who looks straight out at us, while a second woman in a shift bathes in the stream behind. A basket of fruit, a loaf and the woman's discarded blue dress lie in the corner. The pose is borrowed from a Renaissance engraving after Raphael, and the subject from a Giorgione in the Louvre, but Manet painted it flat and bright, with hardly any modelling, and gave the nude the face of his model Victorine Meurent, which is what offended. The Salon jury rejected it, and it hung instead at the Salon des Refusés that Napoleon III allowed that spring, where it was the most ridiculed picture in the show. The younger painters who became the Impressionists took it as a declaration that a picture need not tell a story or pretend to be a window. Monet began his own huge Déjeuner sur l'herbe in reply two years later. The canvas is over two and a half metres wide.
facts: Rejected by the Salon jury of 1863 and shown at the Salon des Refusés, which opened on 15 May 1863.

The composition follows Marcantonio Raimondi's engraving of The Judgement of Paris after Raphael; the models were Victorine Meurent, Manet's brother Gustave or Eugène, and his future brother-in-law Ferdinand Leenhoff.
Manet called it Le Bain; the present title dates from 1867.

artworks.title: Maxwell's equations

date.label: 1865 (A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field)

artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Electricity, magnetism and light in four lines: charges make electric fields, there are no magnetic charges, a changing magnetic field makes an electric one, and currents or changing electric fields make magnetic ones. Maxwell read the theory to the Royal Society in December 1864 and published it in 1865; from the equations fell a wave travelling at the speed of light, so light had to be an electromagnetic wave. Radio, the transistor further along, and every screen this museum is seen on, follow from here.
facts: Maxwell's own paper had twenty equations in twenty variables; the four vector equations shown are Oliver Heaviside's recasting of 1884 and 1885.
Heinrich Hertz produced and detected the predicted waves in 1887, eight years after Maxwell's death, and said they were of no use whatsoever.
Einstein kept a portrait of Maxwell on his study wall, beside Faraday and Newton, and called the theory 'the most profound and fruitful that physics has experienced since Newton'.

artworks.title: The Cradle
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: A young mother sits beside a cradle hung with white muslin and looks down at her sleeping baby, one hand at her cheek, the other holding the edge of the curtain. The light comes through the gauze so that the child is only half seen, and the whole right of the picture is a cascade of white, painted in long transparent strokes. The woman is Edma, Berthe Morisot's sister and until her marriage her painting companion; the baby is Edma's daughter Blanche, born in late 1871. Morisot showed the canvas at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, the only woman among the founders of the group, and kept it when it did not sell. It is the first of her pictures of mothers and children, a subject she took from her own household as the men of the group took boulevards and railway stations. The Louvre bought it from the family in 1930.
facts: Shown at the first Impressionist exhibition in April 1874; Morisot was the only woman among the exhibitors.
The sitters are the painter's sister Edma Pontillon and Edma's daughter Blanche, a few months old.
Morisot had married Eugène Manet, the painter's brother, by the time the picture was sold; it stayed in the family until 1930.

artworks.title: Impression, Sunrise
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: A small orange sun hangs in grey-blue mist over the harbour of Le Havre, its reflection a few broken strokes of red on the water. Two rowing boats are dark shapes in the foreground; behind them, masts, cranes and smoking chimneys dissolve into the haze. Monet painted it in a single sitting from a hotel window in November 1872, working so quickly that the canvas shows through in places. When it was shown at the first independent group exhibition in Paris in 1874, the critic Louis Leroy mocked its title in a satirical review headed 'Exhibition of the Impressionists', and the painters adopted the insult as their name. The picture is therefore the one that gave Impressionism its label. It is less a view than a record of a moment of light, which is what the group was after. Stolen from the Musée Marmottan in 1985, it was recovered in Corsica in 1990 and has hung there since.
facts: Shown in April 1874 at the first Impressionist exhibition, in the former studio of the photographer Nadar on the boulevard des Capucines.
Louis Leroy's review in Le Charivari, 'Exhibition of the Impressionists', gave the movement its name.
Astronomical analysis of the sun's height and the tide dates the view to about 7:35 am on 13 November 1872.
Stolen in October 1985 with eight other paintings and recovered in Corsica in December 1990.

artworks.title: The Galton board
artworks.medium: Balls and pegs, simulated live
artworks.description:
Balls drop through rows of pegs, bouncing left or right at each with even odds, and pile up below. Each ball's fate is pure chance; the pile is not. It settles every time into the same bell-shaped curve, the normal distribution, because the sum of many small independent chances always does: that is the central limit theorem, and Francis Galton built this board in 1873 to make it something you could see. He called it the quincunx, after the pattern of the pegs. It is the shape of measurement error, of heights in a population, of noise in a signal, and the reason so much of statistics assumes a bell.

The balls are falling now, each one a fresh throw of the dice and not a film of one. The dashed line over the pile is the curve the arithmetic predicts; they are finding it on their own.
facts: Twelve rows of pegs give thirteen bins; the odds of the far bins are one in 4,096.
Galton showed the board at the Royal Institution in 1874.
He also used it to argue, wrongly as it turned out, that human traits must revert to the mean of a fixed population.
The same curve appears when the pegs are replaced by anything random enough: dice, rounding errors, the heights of soldiers.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/galton.ts: each ball takes twelve coin-flip turns through the pegs and lands in a bin; the binomial curve is drawn over the pile and the board empties when a bin fills. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: The Ballet Class
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: The end of a class in a rehearsal room of the Paris Opera. The old ballet master Jules Perrot, in a loose grey suit, leans on his long stick and watches one dancer finish a step; the others wait, stretch, scratch their backs, adjust a ribbon or fan themselves, and their mothers sit against the far wall. The floor runs away in a steep diagonal and a watering can, used to damp the boards against dust, stands in the corner. Degas took the room from the old Opera on the rue Le Peletier, which burned down in 1873 while he was working on the picture, and painted every figure from drawings made in his studio. He showed the canvas, begun in 1873 and reworked until 1876, at the second Impressionist exhibition in 1876. Unlike Monet he had no interest in landscape or in painting outdoors; what he shared with the group was the ordinary, unposed moment, seen as if by someone who happened to be standing at the door.
facts: Jules Perrot (1810–1892), the ballet master shown, had been one of the great dancers and choreographers of the Romantic ballet.
Commissioned by the opera singer and collector Jean-Baptiste Faure, who had to wait until 1876 for it.
Shown at the second Impressionist exhibition in 1876; bequeathed to the state by Count Isaac de Camondo in 1911.
A close variant of the same composition is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

artworks.title: Woman with a Parasol
artworks.titleOriginal: La Promenade. La Femme à l'ombrelle
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: Seen from below against a windy sky, a woman in a white dress turns on the crest of a meadow, a green parasol tilted over her shoulder and her veil blowing across her face. Her shadow falls on the grass towards us; a small boy in a straw hat stands further off, half hidden by the slope. The woman is Camille, Monet's wife, and the boy their son Jean, aged seven. Monet painted the canvas outdoors in a single session near their house at Argenteuil in the summer of 1875, which is why the brushwork is so fast: the clouds, the flowers and the folds of the dress are all made of the same quick strokes, and the underside of the parasol takes the green of the grass. It was shown at the second Impressionist exhibition in 1876. Camille died in 1879; Monet repainted the pose twice in 1886 with a model, faces turned away, and those two canvases are in the Musée d'Orsay. The woman is Camille Monet, the child their son Jean.
facts: Shown at the second Impressionist exhibition in April 1876 under the title La Promenade.
Camille Doncieux, Monet's model since 1865 and wife from 1870, died in 1879 at the age of 32.
Monet revisited the composition in 1886 with two 'Essai de figure en plein air' canvases, now in the Musée d'Orsay.

artworks.title: Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette
artworks.titleOriginal: Bal du moulin de la Galette
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: A Sunday afternoon at the open-air dance hall by the old windmill on the hill of Montmartre. Couples turn under the trees and the gas lamps, and in the foreground young women in striped dresses sit at a table with Renoir's friends, who posed for him. Sunlight comes through the leaves in patches, falling as pink and violet spots on a jacket, a hat, the ground. That dappled light, painted exactly as it fell rather than smoothed over, is what made the picture modern: critics in 1877 complained that the dancers looked as if they were covered in mould. The canvas is large, 131 by 175 cm, and Renoir worked on it on the spot, renting a studio nearby and carrying it to the garden with help. It was shown at the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877 and bought by the painter Gustave Caillebotte, whose bequest brought it to the French state in 1894. The crowd is of working Montmartre: seamstresses, florists, painters and writers.
facts: Exhibited at the third Impressionist exhibition in April 1877.
The models were Renoir's friends: the painters Franc-Lamy and Norbert Goeneutte, the writer Georges Rivière, and the sisters Estelle and Jeanne Samary among the women.
Part of Gustave Caillebotte's bequest of 1894; entered the Louvre in 1896 and the Musée d'Orsay in 1986.

artworks.title: Boltzmann's entropy formula
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Entropy is the logarithm of the number of ways, W, that the atoms of a system can be arranged without changing what it looks like from outside. With this, Boltzmann, then a professor in Graz, explained in 1877 why heat flows one way and why the second law of thermodynamics is a law of probability: there are simply far more disordered arrangements than ordered ones. It is the bridge between the world of atoms, which most physicists of his day did not believe in, and the world of steam engines.
facts: The formula in this form, with the constant k, was first written down by Max Planck in 1900; Planck named k Boltzmann's constant.
It is carved on Boltzmann's gravestone in Vienna's Zentralfriedhof.
Boltzmann fought the sceptics of atoms for decades; Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion, and Perrin's experiments, settled the matter soon after his death.

artworks.title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
artworks.titleOriginal: Rue de Paris, temps de pluie
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: A wet afternoon at a crossroads in the new quarter behind the Gare Saint-Lazare. A couple under one umbrella walk towards us, the man in a top hat and frock coat, the woman veiled; a third figure, cut off by the frame, is about to collide with them, and the cobbles shine with rain all the way back to the wedge-shaped apartment block in the distance. The painting is nearly three metres wide and the figures in front are life size, so a visitor stands on the same pavement. Caillebotte, a wealthy engineer-painter who financed the group's exhibitions and bought his friends' pictures, showed it at the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877 with Renoir's Moulin de la Galette. Its careful perspective and smooth finish are not Monet's broken touch, but its subject, the ordinary modern city seen at an odd angle like a photograph, is the Impressionist subject exactly. The street layout is Haussmann's Paris, barely twenty years old when it was painted.
facts: Shown at the third Impressionist exhibition in April 1877, which Caillebotte largely organised and paid for.
The crossroads is the Place de Dublin, where the rue de Turin, rue de Moscou and rue Clapeyron meet; the buildings still stand.
212.2 by 276.2 cm, the largest canvas Caillebotte painted; bought by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1964.
Caillebotte's bequest of 1894 gave the French state the Impressionist paintings now at the heart of the Musée d'Orsay.

artworks.title: The Horse in Motion
artworks.titleOriginal: The Horse in Motion. "Sallie Gardner," owned by Leland Stanford; running at a 1:40 gait over the Palo Alto track, 19th June 1878

madeIn.name: Palo Alto Stock Farm (Leland Stanford's farm, now the Stanford campus)

artworks.medium: Twelve wet-plate photographs taken by electrically tripped cameras, published as a cabinet card; shown here as a reconstructed silent animation
artworks.description: On 19 June 1878, at Leland Stanford's stock farm at Palo Alto, Eadweard Muybridge lined up twelve cameras along a track, each with a shutter tripped by a thread the horse broke as it passed. The mare Sallie Gardner, running at about forty kilometres an hour, took the twelve pictures herself in under half a second. Stanford wanted to settle an old argument: does a galloping horse ever have all four feet off the ground? The plates showed that it does, but with the legs gathered under the body, not stretched out fore and aft as painters had always drawn them. Muybridge sold the sequence as a cabinet card and, from 1880, spun the frames on a glass disc in his zoopraxiscope so that audiences could watch the horse run. That projector is a direct ancestor of cinema, and the stop-motion study of movement he began here filled the eleven volumes of Animal Locomotion in 1887. What is shown here is a modern animation of the eleven usable frames of the 1878 card.
facts: The exposures were about a thousandth of a second, far faster than any studio portrait of the day.
Stanford paid for the work; the legend that it settled a $25,000 bet is unproven.
Muybridge's zoopraxiscope projections of 1880 were among the first moving pictures shown to a paying public.
Muybridge had been acquitted of murdering his wife's lover in 1875, three years before this sequence.

artworks.title: The Child's Bath
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: A woman in a striped dress holds a child on her lap and washes its feet in a basin of water, both of them looking down at the foot in her hand. We look down too, from above, so that the floor, the carpet, the chest of drawers and the jug tip up towards us and the picture is nearly all pattern: stripes, flowers on the wallpaper, lozenges on the rug. The steep view and the flat shapes come from the Japanese woodcuts Cassatt had seen at a large exhibition in Paris in 1890, which changed her work. She was an American from Pittsburgh who settled in Paris in 1874, was invited by Degas to show with the Impressionists and did so four times. Mothers and children were her subject for thirty years, treated without sentiment; here the child's body has real weight and the mother's grip is firm. The Art Institute of Chicago bought the painting in 1910.
facts: Shown at Cassatt's first solo exhibition, at Durand-Ruel in Paris in November 1893, as La Toilette de l'enfant.
The high viewpoint and flat patterning follow the Japanese prints shown at the École des Beaux-Arts in 1890; Cassatt made her own set of ten colour prints in reply in 1890–91.
Cassatt exhibited with the Impressionists in 1879, 1880, 1881 and 1886, the only American to do so.
100.3 by 66.1 cm; bought by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1910, the first of her paintings in a Chicago museum.

artworks.title: Lilienthal Normalsegelapparat
artworks.medium: Hang glider: willow and bamboo frame covered with waxed cotton, folding wings
artworks.description: The first aircraft ever produced in series and sold: Otto Lilienthal's 'normal soaring apparatus' of 1894, a hang glider of willow, bamboo and waxed cotton weighing 20 kg, which he flew from an artificial hill he built in Berlin-Lichterfelde and from the Gollenberg near Stölln. Lilienthal made some two thousand glides in his machines, the first repeated, controlled flights by a human being, and sold at least nine of this model for 500 marks each. He died on 10 August 1896, the day after a crash in one. This is a scan of the Deutsches Museum's replica, built by the museum in 1958 after the original from Lilienthal's estate had decayed.
facts: The Wright brothers began with Lilienthal's tables of lift; the 1903 Flyer in the next row is where his line of work led.
Buyers of the production glider included Nikolai Zhukovsky in Moscow and the publisher William Randolph Hearst; originals survive in London, Washington and Moscow.
The pilot hung by the forearms in the frame and steered by swinging the body; the wings fold for transport, and a bow at the front cushioned crashes.

artworks.title: Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat
artworks.titleOriginal: L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat

date.label: first shown 25 January 1896, Lyon; this print is the summer 1897 remake (Lumière catalogue no. 653)

artworks.medium: 35 mm silent film, about 50 seconds, shot with the Cinématographe Lumière
artworks.description: Fifty seconds, one fixed camera, no cut: a steam train pulls into the station at La Ciotat, on the coast east of Marseille where the Lumière family had a summer house, and passengers step down onto the platform. Louis Lumière set the Cinématographe at the platform's edge so that the locomotive grows from a speck to fill the frame and passes within arm's reach, a diagonal that still makes audiences lean back. The story that the first viewers fled screaming is a legend; the film was not even on the programme of the Lumières' first public show in Paris on 28 December 1895, and was first screened in Lyon in January 1896. It was popular enough that the brothers reshot it twice on the same platform; the version seen here, catalogue number 653, was taken in the summer of 1897 with Lumière children among the waiting passengers. The Cinématographe weighed five kilograms, was cranked by hand, and served as camera, printer and projector.
facts: Shown at about 16 frames a second from a reel of 17 metres: the length of one Lumière film.
Auguste and Louis Lumière ran their father's photographic-plate factory in Lyon; the camera was patented in February 1895.
By 1897 the Lumière catalogue listed over a thousand 'views' shot by operators across the world.
The film entered the public domain in France only on 1 January 2025, seventy years after Auguste Lumière's death.

artworks.title: The Boulevard Montmartre at Night
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: The boulevard Montmartre seen from a hotel window at night, the wet roadway catching the glow of gas lamps, cab lanterns and lit shop windows, which run off in two converging rows of yellow and white dabs under a dark blue sky. Nothing is drawn: the carriages, the crowd on the pavements and the lamps are all touches of colour on a blue-grey ground. Pissarro, the oldest of the Impressionists and the only one to show at all eight of their exhibitions, took a room at the Grand Hôtel de Russie in February 1897, when an eye infection kept him indoors, and painted the boulevard fourteen times in two months, in morning mist, in sun, in rain, during Mardi Gras and here after dark. It is the only night scene of the series. The picture was not exhibited in his lifetime; his son Lucien gave it to the National Gallery in 1925.
facts: One of fourteen views of the boulevard Montmartre painted from the same window between February and April 1897.
The only night view in the series, and never exhibited during Pissarro's life.
Pissarro showed at all eight Impressionist exhibitions from 1874 to 1886, the only painter to do so.

artworks.title: The Water-Lily Pond
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas
artworks.description: An arched wooden footbridge, painted pale green, crosses a pond so thick with lily pads that almost no open water shows. Willows and tall grasses close off the sky, so the whole square canvas is green, blue and pink, lit from above. This is the water garden Monet made at Giverny after 1893, diverting a stream to fill the pond and planting water lilies; he built the bridge in the Japanese style he knew from the prints he collected. In the summer of 1899 he painted the bridge from the same spot about twelve times, in a series he showed at Durand-Ruel's gallery in 1900, and this canvas, bought by the National Gallery in 1927, is one of them. It marks the point at which the garden became his only subject. Over the next quarter century the bridge disappeared from the pictures and the surface of the pond took over, ending in the panels of the Orangerie.
facts: One of about twelve views of the Japanese bridge painted in the summer of 1899; others are in the Musée d'Orsay, the Metropolitan Museum and Philadelphia.
Monet dug the pond in 1893 on land across the road and railway from his house, and planted it with hybrid water lilies.

artworks.title: Maple Leaf Rag
artworks.medium: Rag for solo piano; printed sheet music
artworks.description: Scott Joplin, the son of a formerly enslaved railway labourer, was playing piano in the Maple Leaf Club in Sedalia, Missouri, when the local music dealer John Stark published his 'Maple Leaf Rag' in September 1899. Joplin's contract gave him a royalty of one cent a copy, unusual for a Black composer at the time, and the piece went on to sell hundreds of thousands of copies, the first instrumental sheet music to do so. Its four sixteen-bar strains, with a syncopated right hand bouncing over a steady marching left hand, became the pattern for classic ragtime and the first distinctly American popular music to spread around the world. The cover shown is the 1899 Sedalia first edition. The visitor hears the United States Marine Band's 1906 recording, among the earliest ever made of the piece, which as a pre-1926 federal recording is in the public domain.
facts: Joplin's royalty contract with Stark, signed on 10 August 1899, is one of the earliest surviving royalty agreements for a Black American composer.
Joplin himself recorded the rag on piano rolls in 1916, a year before his death, when illness had already affected his playing.
The rag was published in Sedalia; Stark moved his firm to St. Louis the next year as sales took off.

artworks.title: A Trip to the Moon

location.name: Paris
location.institution: Cinémathèque française and others; the only known hand-coloured print was restored by Lobster Films in 2011

artworks.medium: 35 mm silent film, about 14 minutes at 14 frames a second, 260 metres, with painted sets and in-camera effects
artworks.description: Six astronomers are fired from a giant cannon in a bullet-shaped shell, land in the eye of the Man in the Moon, fight the Selenites with umbrellas, and fall back to Earth to a hero's welcome. Georges Méliès, a Paris stage magician who had bought a projector in 1896, made it in his glass-walled studio at Montreuil over the summer of 1902, playing the lead astronomer himself and painting the cardboard Moon. At fourteen minutes and thirty tableaux it was the longest and most expensive film he had attempted, and it was his biggest success, sold worldwide and pirated almost at once in the United States by Thomas Edison's agents. The shot of the shell stuck in the Moon's eye has become the emblem of early cinema. Méliès's business collapsed in the 1910s; he burned many of his negatives and ended up selling toys at the Gare Montparnasse before he was rediscovered and honoured in 1929. A hand-coloured print, found in Barcelona in 1993, was restored in 2011.
facts: Loosely based on Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon (1865) and H. G. Wells's The First Men in the Moon (1901).
Méliès used stop-substitution, dissolves and painted perspective; the Moon's approach was done by moving the camera on a trolley toward a painted face.
Edison's company copied the film and sold it in America without paying Méliès a cent, a loss he complained of all his life.
The film was added to the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2002, its centenary year.

artworks.title: Wright Flyer

location.name: National Air and Space Museum, Washington, D.C.
location.institution: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

artworks.medium: Aircraft: spruce and ash airframe covered in muslin, cast-aluminium crankcase engine
artworks.description: The Wright Flyer is the biplane in which Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained, controlled flights of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903. Built in the brothers' Dayton bicycle shop, it combined a wing-warping control system with a purpose-built 12-horsepower petrol engine and twin pusher propellers. This is the Smithsonian's laser scan of the original aircraft as it hangs in the National Air and Space Museum.
facts: Four flights were made on 17 December 1903; the longest covered 852 ft (260 m) in 59 seconds.
The 12-horsepower engine was built from scratch in six weeks by the Wrights' mechanic Charlie Taylor, with a cast-aluminium crankcase.
The Flyer joined the Smithsonian collection in 1948 after a long dispute between Orville Wright and the Institution over who flew first.

artworks.title: Gauhar Jaan sings a thumri
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a thumri in raga Gara
artworks.description: On 8 November 1902, in a Calcutta hotel room, Gauhar Jaan sang into Fred Gaisberg's horn and ended with the words 'My name is Gauhar Jaan': the first recording made in India by an Indian artist. Two years later the Gramophone Company came back and recorded her again; this thumri in raga Gara is from that 1904 session. She was the subcontinent's first gramophone star, cut some six hundred sides in a dozen languages, charged three thousand rupees a session and toured in a carriage with a retinue. Before her, a performance in Calcutta ended when the singer stopped. After her, it could be heard in Madras, in London, and a hundred and twenty years later here. The piece is 'Aan baan jiya mein lago'.
facts: The 1902 sessions used wax masters shipped to Hanover for pressing; the first Indian discs went on sale in 1903.
She recorded in Hindustani, Bengali, Persian, Arabic, English and more, usually ending with her spoken name so the Hanover engineers could label the record.
Her thumri style, light-classical and emotional, was the gramophone's first Indian idiom.

artworks.title: Clair de lune
artworks.medium: Piece for solo piano, third movement of the Suite bergamasque; engraved first edition
artworks.description: Debussy sketched the four pieces of his Suite bergamasque around 1890, when he was twenty-eight and almost unknown, but he put them aside. Fifteen years later, now famous for Pelléas et Mélisande and La mer, he was persuaded by the publisher Fromont to revise and release them, and the suite appeared in Paris in 1905. The third piece, originally called 'Promenade sentimentale', was renamed 'Clair de lune' after a poem by Paul Verlaine in which masked revellers sing 'in the calm moonlight, sad and beautiful'. Its hushed opening in D-flat major, with chords that float rather than progress, became the best-known example of the new harmonic language later called impressionist, and one of the most loved piano pieces ever written. The page shown is the first page of the 1905 Fromont edition. The visitor hears the piece played by the Dutch pianist Laurens Goedhart, who released his 2011 recording under a Creative Commons Attribution licence.
facts: The title comes from Verlaine's poem 'Clair de lune' in Fêtes galantes (1869), which Debussy also set twice as a song.
The word 'bergamasque' refers to a rustic dance from Bergamo mentioned in the same poem.
Debussy never recorded the piece; his few piano rolls, made in 1913, are of other works.

artworks.title: Bangalore Nagarathnamma sings a Dikshitar kriti
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a kriti by Muthuswami Dikshitar
artworks.description: One of the first Carnatic recordings ever made, from the Gramophone Company's 1905 Madras sessions, and the voice is that of a remarkable woman. Nagarathnamma was a devadasi, a Sanskrit scholar, a singer who performed for the Mysore court, and later the richest musician in Madras; she spent that fortune building the memorial over Tyagaraja's grave at Thiruvaiyaru and founding the Aradhana festival there, which is still the largest gathering in Carnatic music. In 1910 she published the erotic Telugu poem Radhika Santvanam by the eighteenth-century poet Muddupalani, and fought the colonial government's ban on it. The kriti here is by Muthuswami Dikshitar, one of the trinity of Carnatic composers, sung as a garland of ragas.
facts: The 1905 Madras sessions were the Gramophone & Typewriter Company's first in South India.
Her edition of Radhika Santvanam was banned in 1911 and not freely published again until 1947.
The Tyagaraja Aradhana she founded is held each January on the banks of the Kaveri.

artworks.title: Sun Juxian sings Peking opera
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a xipi aria of the Peking opera
artworks.description: One of the three great old-man voices of the Peking opera, recorded at sixty-four when the gramophone first reached China. Sun Juxian was, with Tan Xinpei and Wang Guifen, among the laosheng who fixed the mature style of the jingju in the last decades of the Qing; he had been a soldier before he was a singer, and his delivery kept something of the parade ground. 'Zhongchen bu pa si', a loyal minister does not fear death, is a xipi aria, the brighter of the opera's two melodic modes, sung over the jinghu fiddle. Victor's first expedition to China cut it in 1905; what survives is a later Victor reissue, re-recorded from a worn disc, and the hiss is the price of hearing him at all.
facts: Victor's 1905 Chinese catalogue was the first commercial recording of the Peking opera.
The laosheng role, the dignified older man, is sung in a natural voice, unlike the falsetto dan.
He lived to ninety, long enough to see Mei Lanfang make the opera a world art.

artworks.title: Mass–energy equivalence
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Mass and energy are the same thing in different units, and the exchange rate is the speed of light squared. Einstein, a 26-year-old examiner at the Swiss patent office in Bern, derived it in a three-page afterthought to his special relativity paper, received by Annalen der Physik on 27 September 1905. The rate is so large that the mass lost by the Sun each second lights the Earth, and a gram of matter, fully converted, would power a city for a day.
facts: Einstein's paper is titled 'Does the inertia of a body depend on its energy content?' and writes the relation as L/V², with L for energy and V for the speed of light; the form E = mc² came later.
1905 was Einstein's annus mirabilis: four papers, on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity and this.
The first direct test came in 1932, when Cockcroft and Walton split lithium nuclei and found the energy released matched the mass lost.

artworks.title: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies

location.institution: Printed journal (Annalen der Physik vol. 17, pp. 891-921); this scan is the Internet Archive's serials microfilm copy sim_annalen-der-physik_1905_17_5

artworks.medium: Letterpress printing on paper, journal page
artworks.description: The first page of the paper in which a twenty-six-year-old patent clerk in Bern replaced Newton's absolute space and time. Einstein starts from an everyday puzzle: moving a magnet past a coil or the coil past the magnet gives the same current, yet the physics of the day described the two cases differently. From that he takes two assumptions, that the laws of physics are the same for every observer moving at constant speed and that light travels at the same speed for all of them, and works out the consequences in thirty pages: moving clocks run slow, moving rods shrink, events simultaneous for one observer are not for another, and nothing with mass reaches the speed of light. The paper cites no earlier work and thanks only his friend Michele Besso. It reached the Annalen der Physik on 30 June 1905 and appeared on 26 September; a three-page sequel in November added the equation later written as E = mc². The theory became known as special relativity when Einstein generalised it to gravity in 1915.
facts: One of four papers Einstein published in 1905, his 'miracle year', alongside the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and E = mc².
Written outside any university: Einstein was a 'technical expert, third class' at the Swiss patent office.
The word 'relativity' appears only as the 'principle of relativity'; Einstein did not name the theory.
The equations rediscovered Lorentz's transformations but gave them a wholly new meaning: there is no ether and no absolute rest.

artworks.title: Toyotake Roshō sings gidayū
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; gidayū-bushi, voice and shamisen
artworks.description: The pop star of Meiji Japan. Gidayū-bushi is the chanted narration of the puppet theatre, voice and shamisen telling the story and playing every part; in the 1890s young women took it up as a concert art, musume-gidayū, and became the first mass popular music of modern Japan, with fan clubs, riots and newspaper gossip. Toyotake Roshō of Osaka was the biggest of them. When the Gramophone Company's recording expedition reached Japan in 1906, she was among the first they cut, and this is that disc: the scene at Tsubosaka temple from an 1879 play, in which the blind Sawaichi and his wife are saved by the Kannon. It is one of the oldest recordings of Japanese music that can be heard anywhere.
facts: The 1906-07 Gaisberg expedition made some 270 Japanese recordings, the first large body of them.
Musume-gidayū drew student audiences so fervent that the police treated them as a public-order problem.
The puppet theatre itself, bunraku, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

artworks.title: Caruso sings 'Vesti la giubba'

date.label: 17 March 1907 (recording session, Victor Talking Machine Company)

artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; aria from Leoncavallo's Pagliacci (1892)
artworks.description: The accomplishment here is not the aria but the record. On 17 March 1907 the Neapolitan tenor Enrico Caruso stood before a recording horn in the Victor Talking Machine Company's studio and sang 'Vesti la giubba', the clown Canio's lament from Leoncavallo's Pagliacci, in which he must put on his costume and make the audience laugh while his heart breaks. The disc is generally reckoned the first gramophone record to sell a million copies. Caruso's warm, powerful voice suited the crude acoustic process better than anyone else's, and his Victor Red Seal discs, sold at premium prices, persuaded the public that a phonograph belonged in the home. He became the first star made by recordings, earning more from records than from the stage. The photograph, from the Bain News Service, shows him listening to a Victrola. The visitor hears the 1907 recording itself, now in the public domain.
facts: Caruso made his first records in a Milan hotel room in 1902 for the Gramophone Company; he recorded 'Vesti la giubba' three times, in 1902, 1904 and 1907.
His Victor contract eventually guaranteed him $100,000 a year, and his records are said to have earned him some two million dollars over his career.
All United States sound recordings made before 1923 entered the public domain on 1 January 2022 under the Music Modernization Act.

artworks.title: 'Abd al-Hayy Hilmi sings a qasida
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a qasida with takht
artworks.description: The most popular singer in Egypt in the first decade of the century, in a form the gramophone could barely hold. 'Abd al-Hayy Hilmi was the wild one of the Nahda, a drinker and a genius, who would stop a performance when the mood left him and sing for an hour when it came; he died at fifty-five in 1912. The qasida is the oldest Arab song form, a classical poem sung line by line with the singer improvising on each, and here he has behind him the violin of Sami al-Shawwa, 'the prince of the violin', then at the start of a career that lasted into the age of Umm Kulthum. The side was cut in Cairo around 1909 and pressed a decade later in New York for the Arab communities of the Americas. The label stands in for a portrait.
facts: Opera Disc of New York reissued the Gramophone Company's Arab masters without licence in the early 1920s; it is why many survive.
Sami al-Shawwa (1885-1965) later accompanied Umm Kulthum and toured the Americas.
The Nahda singers' improvisation, the layali and mawwal, is the ancestor of the long tarab performances of the mid-century.

artworks.title: Antonio Chacón sings a malagueña
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; malagueña, cante with guitar
artworks.description: The central figure of flamenco's classical age, from his first session. Antonio Chacón of Jerez was called Don Antonio in his lifetime, the only cantaor given the title; he had an unusually high, sweet voice, and used it to turn the malagueñas, granaínas and cartageneras into the long, ornamented forms that every singer since has measured themselves against. He sang in the Madrid cafés for thirty years and for the King, and his records, made in four blocks between 1908 and 1928, are the first great body of recorded cante. This malagueña is from the first of them, for Odeón, with the Granada guitarist Habichuela. The image is the bust of him in Jerez; no portrait of him is free to use.
facts: He was the first flamenco singer to earn a fortune, and the first to lose one.
His pupil and rival was Manuel Vallejo; his guitarist in later years was Ramón Montoya.
The malagueña de Chacón is still a named style, sung as he set it.

artworks.title: Yusuf al-Manyalawi sings 'Sahi al-jufun'
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a dawr of the Nahda repertoire
artworks.description: The summit of the Egyptian Nahda, the renaissance of Arab art music in the last decades of the nineteenth century, caught on a twelve-inch disc two years before the singer's death. Yusuf al-Manyalawi was a Sufi shaykh of the Mevlevi order and a Quran reciter before he was the most admired singer in Cairo; the Gramophone Company paid him more than any other artist in the Arab world and recorded him between 1905 and 1910 with the finest takht of the day, led by the qanun player Muhammad al-'Aqqad. Here he opens 'Sahi al-jufun', the singers of the chorus answering him, improvising on the maqam in the way that was lost when the song form shortened to fit three-minute records. The disc's own label stands in for a portrait.
facts: His recordings were reissued in the 1920s by the Opera Disc Company of New York for the Arab diaspora.
The Nahda singers improvised within a dawr for twenty minutes or more; a twelve-inch disc gave them four.
The AMAR Foundation in Lebanon has reissued his complete recordings on ten CDs.

Coimbatore Thayi, a devadasi from the Coimbatore temple tradition, was the Gramophone Company's best-selling South Indian artist of the 1910s and the first Tamil singer given a recording session of her own, in Madras in 1910. Her records were sold as far as Paris, where Maurice Delage heard them and wrote his Quatre poèmes hindous around her voice. The disc's own label stands in for a portrait; none that is free to use survives.

The Tevaram, with the Tiruvachakam, make up the Tamil Shaiva canon, the Panniru Tirumurai.
Delage's 1912 Quatre poèmes hindous, with their imitated vocal slides, were his attempt to write what he heard on her records.

artworks.title: Juan Breva sings malagueñas
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; malagueñas, cante with guitar
artworks.description: The oldest voice in flamenco. Juan Breva was born in Vélez-Málaga in 1844, so he was singing in the cafés cantantes when the art was being made, before the word flamenco meant what it means now; he sang for Alfonso XII at the palace and was the first cantaor to be famous across Spain. His malagueñas, the cante of his own country, is the form he made his own, slow and ornamented over the guitar. He recorded it in Madrid in 1910 at sixty-six, one of the handful of sessions that carry the sound of the nineteenth century into ours; Lorca wrote a poem about him, blind and singing, 'with the voice of a girl'.
facts: He is said to have been the first flamenco singer to perform standing up, with the guitar played for him rather than by him.
Lorca's 'Juan Breva' is in the Poema del cante jondo of 1921.
He died poor in Málaga in 1918; the city named a peña after him.

artworks.title: A gazel with ney, Constantinople

creators.name: Hafız Tevfik Efendi and Safinaz Hanım

artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a gazel, two voices and ney
artworks.description: Ottoman music in the last years of the empire. The gazel is the Turkish art of improvising a classical poem over a drone, the singer finding the maqam as he goes; here two voices trade it, a hafız, a man who has the Quran by heart and sings as part of that training, and a woman, Safinaz Hanım, one of the first Ottoman women to make records, over the breathy reed flute of the Mevlevi dervishes, the ney. Odeon's Constantinople catalogue of the years before the First World War is the founding corpus of recorded Turkish music, cut in the city while it was still the Ottoman capital. The disc's own label stands in for a portrait. The singers are Hafız Tevfik Efendi and Safinaz Hanım.
facts: The ney is the instrument of Rumi's Masnavi, which opens with its lament at being cut from the reed bed.
Odeon's Istanbul recordings were made by the International Talking Machine Company of Berlin until 1911.
Women singers appeared on Ottoman records a generation before they could appear on an Ottoman stage.

artworks.description: Flamenco's greatest female voice, recorded at twenty, with the man who invented the modern flamenco guitar. Pastora Pavón, called La Niña de los Peines after a tango she sang about combs, was from the Alameda in Seville and had been singing in cafés cantantes since she was eight; Lorca and Falla put her at the centre of their 1922 Concurso de Cante Jondo, and in 1999 her recordings were declared a Bien de Interés Cultural, a protected monument of Andalusia, the only sound recordings to be so. The tarantas is the cante of the mining country of Almería and Murcia, free in rhythm, a lament; behind her Ramón Montoya, whose playing turned the guitar from accompaniment into an art of its own. The disc was cut in Madrid about 1910.
facts: Her records with Montoya, made between 1909 and the late 1920s, are the core of the flamenco canon.
The Concurso de Cante Jondo of Granada, 1922, organised by Falla and Lorca, took her as its measure of the cante.
Ramón Montoya's 1936 Paris recordings are the first flamenco guitar solos on disc.

artworks.title: Bohr's atom
artworks.medium: A hydrogen atom, computed live
artworks.description:
An electron is allowed only certain orbits, and when it jumps from one to another it gives off or takes in a flash of light whose colour is fixed by the jump: that was Bohr's idea in 1913, and it explained in one stroke the lines hydrogen had been known to make for fifty years, the red, blue-green and violet of the Balmer series, to four decimal places. It was wrong in its details, there are no orbits, and right in everything that mattered, and it is where quantum theory begins to be about atoms.

The atom here is running, not drawn: the electron runs round its shells and every few seconds a photon comes in and lifts it, or it falls and a photon leaves, in hydrogen's own colours; the fall to the lowest shell is ultraviolet, shown faint and violet.
facts: Balmer found the formula for hydrogen's visible lines in 1885 from four measured wavelengths; he was a schoolteacher in Basel.
The red line, 656 nanometres, is why hydrogen nebulae glow red in photographs.
Bohr was twenty-seven and had been in Rutherford's laboratory in Manchester the year before.
Sommerfeld, then Heisenberg and Schrödinger, replaced the orbits within thirteen years; the energy levels stayed.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/atom.ts: a nucleus, one electron on four allowed shells, and photons in and out coloured by the Rydberg formula for each jump. The shells are spaced to fit, not as n squared. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: Einstein's field equations
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Matter tells spacetime how to curve, and curved spacetime tells matter how to move. The left side is the geometry of spacetime, the right its content of matter and energy; the line stands for ten coupled equations. Einstein presented them to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin on 25 November 1915, after eight years of work and a final month of racing David Hilbert. They replaced Newton's law a few rows back, and they describe black holes, the expanding universe and the gravitational waves first heard a century later.
facts: Karl Schwarzschild found the first exact solution, the one that describes a black hole, within weeks, while serving in the German army on the Russian front; he died in 1916.
The 1919 solar eclipse expeditions led by Arthur Eddington measured the bending of starlight the equations predict and made Einstein famous overnight.
In 1917 Einstein added a cosmological constant to keep the universe static; it was dropped when Hubble found the expansion, and brought back in 1998 for dark energy.

artworks.title: Manuel Carvalho sings 'Fado da Severa'
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a traditional fado with orchestra
artworks.description: The fado's founding song, about the fado's founding singer. Maria Severa Onofriana, a Lisbon prostitute and guitarist of the Mouraria, died in 1846 at twenty-six and became the genre's legend within a generation; the Fado da Severa, sung to her memory, is the oldest piece in the repertoire still sung. No fado recorded in Lisbon before 1926 can be freely heard today, so this is the oldest fado that can: the Victor company's Portuguese series, cut in Camden, New Jersey, for the emigrant communities of New England, with Manuel Carvalho, Victor's house Portuguese singer from 1916 to 1925, and the studio orchestra where a Lisbon café would have had a guitarra. The painting is José Malhoa's 'O Fado' of 1910, which hangs in the Museu de Lisboa.
facts: Severa's life became a novel in 1901, a play, and in 1931 the first Portuguese sound film, 'A Severa'.
Victor's immigrant catalogues of the 1910s and 20s preserved many traditions their home countries did not record.
Rosario Bourdon, the conductor, was a cellist who led hundreds of Victor sessions in these years.

artworks.title: Sol Plaatje sings 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika'
artworks.medium: Acoustic 78 rpm gramophone recording; a hymn by Enoch Sontonga, 1897
artworks.description: The earliest known recording of 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika', God Bless Africa, the hymn Enoch Sontonga wrote in Johannesburg in 1897 and which became the anthem of the African National Congress in 1925, of the struggle against apartheid, and in 1994 of South Africa itself; it is sung today, in one form or another, by five countries. The singer is not a musician by trade. Solomon Plaatje was a journalist, a novelist, a translator of Shakespeare into Tswana and the first secretary-general of the ANC; he was in London in 1923 campaigning against the Natives Land Act, appearing in a show at the Philharmonic Hall, and used the visit to put the hymn on record, with Sylvia Colenso, a bishop's granddaughter, at the piano.
facts: Sontonga wrote the first verse and the tune in 1897; the poet Samuel Mqhayi added seven more in 1927.
Plaatje's 'Native Life in South Africa' (1916) is the founding document of the land question.
Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe have all used the tune; Namibia's anthem borrows from it.

artworks.title: Ford Model T Runabout
artworks.medium: steel body on wood frame, wooden spoke wheels
artworks.description: The car that put the world on wheels. Ford built more than fifteen million Model Ts between 1908 and 1927, and the moving assembly line at Highland Park cut the price from $780 in 1910 to $290 in 1924, when this two-seat runabout was the cheapest car in the catalogue. Simple, tough and endlessly adaptable, it was voted the most influential car of the twentieth century. This is an artist's reconstruction of the type, not a scan of a particular car.
facts: The assembly line cut the time to build a chassis from twelve and a half hours to ninety-three minutes.
"Any customer can have a car painted any colour that he wants, so long as it is black": from 1914 to 1925, black japan enamel was the only paint that dried fast enough for the line.
The engine ran on petrol, kerosene or ethanol, and farmers belted the rear wheel to saws, pumps and threshers.
Pedals, not a gear lever: the Model T's two-speed planetary transmission was worked with the feet.

artworks.title: Les Nymphéas
artworks.medium: Oil on canvas, four panels glued to the curved walls of an oval room
artworks.description: Step in. Monet spent the last twelve years of his life on these, in a studio he built at Giverny to hold them, painting his pond with no shore and no horizon, only water, lilies, reflected sky and the hanging willows, on canvases two metres tall and up to thirteen metres long. He gave them to France the day after the Armistice of 1918, on condition that they be shown in two oval rooms lit from above, where a visitor would stand surrounded by water, and the Orangerie rooms opened in May 1927, five months after his death. This is the first of the two rooms with its four panels in their places: Setting Sun at the entrance, Clouds to the north, Green Reflections to the east, Morning to the south. Turn in the middle; the pond goes round. His eyes were failing from cataracts as he painted them, and the late colours are partly what he could still see.
facts: Monet called them his 'grandes décorations'; the eight panels in the two rooms run to ninety-one metres of canvas.
He refused to let them leave his studio until they were installed exactly as he had specified, so they arrived after he died.
The rooms were lit by daylight from skylights in 1927, boarded over in the 1960s, and restored to daylight in 2006.
The pond itself still exists at Giverny, dug in 1893 by diverting a branch of the river Epte, over the objections of his neighbours.

artworks.title: The Schrödinger equation
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: How the wave function Ψ of a quantum system changes in time: the Hamiltonian, the system's energy, drives it, with Planck's constant setting the scale. Schrödinger, a professor at the University of Zürich, published wave mechanics in four papers in 1926; the time-dependent form shown here is in the fourth, received on 21 June. It is the equation of chemistry: the periodic table, the shapes of molecules and the behaviour of the electrons in the chips further along this lane all come out of it.
facts: Schrödinger conceived the equation over Christmas 1925 at a villa in Arosa; the first paper reached the Annalen der Physik on 27 January 1926.
Max Born showed the same year that |Ψ|² is a probability, the reading Schrödinger himself never liked.
Schrödinger shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac; his cat, the thought experiment, came in 1935.

contributed.note: Typeset by 20watts from the TeX in the record with MathJax, with a figure drawn for this museum; the rendering is CC0, the equation itself is not subject to copyright.

artworks.title: A Turing machine
artworks.medium: A tape, a head and nine rules, run live
artworks.description:
A tape of cells, a head that reads the one beneath it, and a table of rules: in this state, seeing this symbol, write that, move left or right, go to that state. Alan Turing set this out in 1936, in On Computable Numbers, to pin down what it means to compute something at all. He showed that one such machine can imitate any other given its table on the tape, and that there are questions no machine can settle, whatever the table. Every computer since is this, at bottom.

The machine here is running as you watch, with nine rules. It walks to the end of the number on the tape, adds one in binary carrying to the left, walks home, and does it again; it will count for as long as the museum is open.
facts: Turing's paper was written to answer Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem: no, there is no procedure that decides every mathematical statement.
The universal machine, able to run any other, is the idea of software.
Alonzo Church reached the same limits the same year by a different road; the two are now one thesis.
The number on the tape is shown in decimal above it, and the rule that just fired is marked on the table.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/turing.ts: nine rules add one to a binary number on the tape, over and over, with the firing rule marked on the table. The machine is the museum's own, CC0; the idea is Turing's 1936 paper.

artworks.title: Bombe drums

creators.name: Alan Turing
creators.role: designer (with Gordon Welchman's diagonal board; engineered by Harold Keen, British Tabulating Machine Company)

date.label: 1940 (original design; drums shown are a 1995–2008 rebuild)

location.name: The National Museum of Computing, Bletchley Park

artworks.medium: Electromechanical cipher-breaking machine component: Bakelite and metal rotor drum with 104 wire brushes
artworks.description: The bombe was the electromechanical machine with which Bletchley Park found the daily settings of German Enigma cipher machines. Designed by Alan Turing, refined by Gordon Welchman and engineered by Harold Keen at the British Tabulating Machine Company, each bombe carried 108 spinning drums, every drum wired to mimic one Enigma rotor. The drums shown here belong to the working reconstruction completed at Bletchley Park in 2008; the wartime machines were all broken up after the war. These are from the rebuilt bombe at Bletchley Park.
facts: The first bombe, named 'Victory', was installed in Hut 1 at Bletchley Park on 18 March 1940.
Each bombe was about 7 ft wide, 6 ft 6 in tall and 2 ft deep, weighed about a ton, and had 108 positions for drums arranged in 36 triplets.
Each drum carried 104 wire brushes in four concentric circles of 26, giving two sets of input and output contacts on its mounting plate.

contributed.note: REPLICA: this shows drums on the working bombe rebuilt by John Harper's 'Phoenix' team of the BCS Computer Conservation Society (1994–2008), now at The National Museum of Computing on the Bletchley Park estate. All wartime bombes were dismantled after 1945 and no free photograph of a surviving original drum was found on Commons (Category:Bletchley Park Bombe has 62 files, all of the rebuild or wartime prints) or in the Science Museum Group collection; no 3D scan exists on Smithsonian, Met, SMG or Sketchfab. Chosen because it shows one Enigma-equivalent's three drums beside the bare mounting plates with their 104 contacts, which explains the mechanism; photographed 2011 at Bletchley Park. The physical size of a drum is not given by Wikipedia or the museum, so dimensions are null. artworks.title: V-2

creators.name: Wernher von Braun and the Peenemünde Army Research Centre

date.label: first flight to the edge of space, 3 October 1942

artworks.medium: An artist's 3D model, at true size
artworks.description: The first thing people made that reached space, and a weapon of terror. On 3 October 1942 an A4 rose from Peenemünde on the Baltic to 84 kilometres, the edge of space, on an engine burning alcohol and liquid oxygen with 25 tonnes of thrust, steered by gyroscopes and graphite vanes in its exhaust: every large rocket since is its descendant. Renamed the V-2, Vergeltungswaffe, it was fired at London and Antwerp from September 1944, three thousand of them, killing some nine thousand people; it was built underground at Mittelwerk by concentration-camp prisoners, of whom more died making it than died from it. Its designers went to America and Russia in 1945 and built the rockets that went to the Moon. It stands here at its full fourteen metres.
facts: Fourteen metres tall, 12.5 tonnes fuelled, a tonne of explosive, Mach 4 on arrival: there was no warning and no defence.
About 12,000 forced labourers died building V-2s at Mittelwerk; about 9,000 people were killed by them.
Von Braun, its chief designer and an SS officer, led the Saturn V team twenty years later.
Captured V-2s launched the first photographs of Earth from space, from New Mexico in 1946.

artworks.title: The first transistor

creators.name: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain
creators.role: inventors (Bell Labs, under William Shockley's group)

madeIn.name: Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey

location.name: Nokia Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey

artworks.medium: Germanium point-contact transistor: germanium slab, gold-foil contacts on a plastic wedge, spring, Perspex mount
artworks.description: On 16 December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain of Bell Telephone Laboratories made a slab of germanium amplify an electrical signal by pressing two closely spaced gold contacts against its surface. Their point-contact transistor, demonstrated to Bell executives a week later, was the first working transistor and the ancestor of every semiconductor device since. The device shown is the display at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, generally identified as a replica of the original.
facts: The critical experiment on 16 December 1947 used a block of germanium with two very closely spaced gold contacts held against it by a spring.
Brattain made the two contacts by slitting a strip of gold foil wrapped over the point of a plastic triangle, leaving a gap of less than 0.1 mm.
The invention was demonstrated to Bell Labs management on 23 December 1947 and announced publicly in June 1948.

artworks.title: Shannon entropy

madeIn.name: Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey

artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: How much information a message carries, measured in bits: the average surprise of its symbols. Shannon published it in July 1948 in 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication', the paper that founded information theory, written at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, the building where the transistor a few rows back had been made the winter before. The formula sets the limit for compressing any data and, with his channel theorem, for sending it through noise; every file, call and stream since has lived inside those limits.
facts: The word 'bit' first appeared in print in this paper; Shannon credits John Tukey with coining it.
Shannon said John von Neumann advised him to call the quantity entropy, since 'no one knows what entropy really is, so in a debate you will always have the advantage'.
The paper also proved that error-free communication is possible over a noisy channel up to a definite capacity, which took forty years of coding theory to reach in practice.

artworks.title: The Lorenz attractor
artworks.medium: Three differential equations, integrated live
artworks.description:
Three equations in three variables, boiled down by Edward Lorenz from a model of air rising in a heated layer. Their solutions never settle and never repeat, yet they never leave this shape of two wings, circling one and then, unpredictably, crossing to the other. Lorenz found in 1961 that restarting a weather computation from rounded-off numbers gave a completely different forecast: tiny differences grow exponentially, so a system can be fully determined and still unpredictable. His 1963 paper, Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow, is where chaos begins as a science, and the attractor is its emblem.

The dark tube is a long run of the equations. The red point is flying them now, as you watch and not from a recording, from a slightly different start, and you can watch it choose a wing.
facts: The butterfly effect takes its name from a 1972 talk of Lorenz's: could a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?
The attractor has fractional dimension, about 2.06.
Lorenz's 1963 paper was cited fewer than ten times in its first decade.
Warwick Tucker proved in 2002 that the attractor Lorenz saw on his screen really exists.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/lorenz.ts: a long run of the equations is drawn once as a tube, and a point integrates them with fourth-order Runge-Kutta in real time, trailing its path. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: Saturn V

creators.name: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, under Wernher von Braun

artworks.medium: NASA's 3D model, at true size
artworks.description: The rocket that took people to the Moon: the real one stood 110 metres, a thirty-six storey building, and weighed 2,900 tonnes fuelled, almost all of it kerosene, hydrogen and liquid oxygen. The five F-1 engines of the first stage burned thirteen tonnes of propellant a second and lifted it, at first, slower than a person walks. It flew thirteen times from 1967 to 1973 without losing a crew, took twenty-four people to the Moon and twelve to its surface, and launched Skylab. Nothing as powerful flew again until 2022. It stands here at its full height, off to the east; walk out to its foot and look up.
facts: Three stages: the first burned for two and a half minutes to 68 kilometres; the third fired twice, once to orbit and once, over the Pacific, toward the Moon.
Von Braun's team at Huntsville designed it; Boeing, North American and Douglas built the stages; 400,000 people worked on Apollo at its peak.
Fully fuelled it weighed 2,970 tonnes; the lunar module that landed weighed 15.
Three remain, on their sides, at Houston, Huntsville and the Kennedy Space Center.

artworks.title: Command Module Columbia

location.name: Washington, D.C.
location.institution: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

artworks.medium: aluminium honeycomb, stainless steel honeycomb, ablative heat shield
artworks.description: Columbia is the command module of Apollo 11, the first mission to land humans on the Moon, and the only part of that spacecraft to return to Earth. Michael Collins orbited the Moon alone in it while Armstrong and Aldrin were on the surface; all three rode it home through re-entry on 24 July 1969. The scan shows the exterior as it stands today, with the heat shield charred from re-entry.

Collins named it after Jules Verne's cannon Columbiad and the ship Columbia Rediviva, the first American vessel to circle the globe.
After the flight it toured all fifty state capitals before coming to the Smithsonian in 1971.
The ablative heat shield reached about 2,800 °C during re-entry.

artworks.title: The first step on the Moon

madeIn.name: Tranquility Base, Mare Tranquillitatis, the Moon

location.name: Houston
location.institution: NASA Johnson Space Center (restored broadcast tapes); the camera itself was left on the Moon

artworks.medium: Live slow-scan television, 320 lines at 10 frames a second, scan-converted for broadcast; shown as a silent loop from NASA's 2009 restoration
artworks.description: At 02:56 UTC on 21 July 1969 Neil Armstrong stepped off the footpad of the Lunar Module Eagle onto the Sea of Tranquility, and about 600 million people watched him do it. The pictures came from a small Westinghouse camera mounted upside down on a fold-down equipment bay on the lander's side, which Armstrong released by pulling a lanyard as he climbed down the ladder. It transmitted a slow-scan signal of 320 lines at ten frames a second, received at Goldstone in California and at Honeysuckle Creek and Parkes in Australia, where it was converted for broadcast by pointing an ordinary television camera at a monitor. That double conversion, and the harsh lunar light, give the famous ghostly image. The original slow-scan tapes were later reused and lost; in 2009 NASA gathered the best surviving broadcast recordings and had them cleaned up, and that restoration is what is shown here. Armstrong's words as he stepped down, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind', are the most quoted sentence of the twentieth century.
facts: Armstrong said he intended 'one small step for a man'; the 'a' is not audible in the recording.
The Lunar Module camera had a single 7-pound body, two lenses and no viewfinder; the astronauts aimed it by hand after the first steps.
Buzz Aldrin followed Armstrong down the ladder nineteen minutes later; Michael Collins, orbiting above, could not see the broadcast at all.
The moonwalk lasted two hours and thirty-one minutes and the two men never went more than about sixty metres from the lander.

artworks.title: The Moon

creators.name: NASA, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter team

artworks.medium: A globe, from the LRO colour mosaic, computed live
artworks.description:
The Moon, as people finally saw all of it. For all of history one face was known and the other was not, until a Soviet probe photographed the far side in 1959 and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, circling since 2009, mapped the whole globe in colour at a resolution of a hundred metres. This is that map on a globe you can turn, and, in VR, hold.

The globe turns as you watch. The red dot is Tranquility Base, where Eagle landed on the evening of 20 July 1969, the day this work is placed on. Look up: the night sky here is Houston's that evening, with the Moon a waxing crescent in the west, drawn larger than life so it can be looked at. Two people were standing on it.
facts: The map is the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera's wide-angle colour mosaic, with the poles filled in from its narrow-angle images.
The far side has almost none of the dark plains that make the face we know; it is nearly all bright highland.
On 20 July 1969 the Moon was six days past new, a crescent setting in the west during the moonwalk in the Americas.
The red dot sits on the Sea of Tranquility, 0.67 degrees north, 23.47 degrees east.

credit.author: NASA / Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio

contributed.note: A globe drawn by src/sims/moon.ts with the colour map from NASA's CGI Moon Kit (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera, SVS 4720, lroc_color_poles_4k.tif, public domain as US government work; the 4 k TIFF is kept in data/originals/sky/ and served as public/sky/moon-4k.jpg and moon-2k.jpg). Tranquility Base is marked at 0.674 N, 23.473 E. The same map is on the Moon in the night sky near this work, drawn three degrees wide, six times the real size, lit from a sun below the horizon to the west-north-west so it shows the waxing crescent of the evening of 20 July 1969; the stars are Houston's that night, about 20:30 local.

artworks.title: The Game of Life
artworks.medium: Cellular automaton, computed live
artworks.description:
A grid of cells, each alive or dead. At every tick a living cell with two or three living neighbours stays alive, a dead cell with exactly three is born, and everything else dies or stays empty. That is the whole of it. John Conway worked the rules out by hand with counters on a Go board, looking for the simplest system that was neither dull nor explosive, and Martin Gardner announced it in Scientific American in October 1970. From three rules come gliders that travel, guns that fire them, and patterns that compute: the Game of Life can run any program a computer can.

The slab is running it now, generation by generation as you watch, seeded with a glider gun at the top left and an R-pentomino that takes 1,103 generations to settle; when the board goes still, it starts over.
facts: The rules fit in one sentence; the behaviour has never been fully catalogued.
Gosper's glider gun, found in November 1970, was the first pattern shown to grow without limit.
Life is Turing complete: a computer can be built inside it out of gliders.
Conway said he came to dislike how the game overshadowed the rest of his mathematics.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/life.ts: a 96 by 96 toroidal board seeded with Gosper's glider gun and an R-pentomino, reseeded when it goes still. The rules are Conway's; the program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: Lunar Roving Vehicle

location.name: Munich
location.institution: Deutsches Museum (replica; the originals are on the Moon)

artworks.medium: Electric vehicle: aluminium chassis, four wire-mesh wheels with individual motors, silver-zinc batteries, folding frame
artworks.description: The Lunar Roving Vehicle is the car the last three Apollo crews drove on the Moon. Built by Boeing with General Motors in under two years, it folded into a bay of the lunar module, weighed 210 kg on Earth and ran on silver-zinc batteries, with a motor in each wire-mesh wheel and a navigation system that always pointed the way home. Three were left on the Moon in 1971 and 1972; this is a 3D reconstruction, from scans and the original drawings, of the Deutsches Museum's replica.
facts: On Apollo 15, 16 and 17 the rovers drove a total of about 90 km, and the Apollo 17 crew went 7.6 km from their lander, the furthest humans have walked or driven from safety on another world.
The wheels are woven from zinc-coated piano wire with titanium chevrons for tread, so they would not clog with dust or crack in the cold.
Gene Cernan set the lunar speed record of 18 km/h in the Apollo 17 rover, and its television camera filmed the lunar module's launch.

artworks.title: MOS 6502, the die

creators.name: Chuck Peddle and the MOS Technology design team

artworks.medium: Silicon die, NMOS, photographed through a microscope
artworks.description: The silicon inside the 6502, with the package cut away. Every line was drawn by hand: the layout team, led by Bill Mensch and Rod Orgill, laid out the chip on paper and film with rubylith, and the first run of masks worked well enough to ship. The regular blocks are the decode ROM and registers; the irregular region is the random logic that sequences each instruction. In 2010 the Visual6502 project photographed a die like this one layer by layer and rebuilt the whole processor as a simulation of its transistors, which runs in a browser today.
facts: Roughly 3,500 transistors on about 4 mm by 4 mm of silicon, in an 8-micrometre NMOS process; a modern phone chip has about five million times as many.
The layout was drawn by hand; the hand-drawn masks of the first revision had a bug in the ROR instruction, so early datasheets left it out.
The Visual6502 project (2010) imaged a 6502 die and turned it into a transistor-level simulation anyone can run.

artworks.title: MOS 6502

creators.name: Chuck Peddle and the MOS Technology design team

artworks.medium: 8-bit NMOS microprocessor in a 40-pin dual in-line package
artworks.description: The 6502 is the 8-bit microprocessor that made the personal computer affordable. Chuck Peddle and a small team at MOS Technology, several of them fresh from Motorola's 6800, designed it to sell for $25 when the 6800 and Intel's 8080 cost around $179, and introduced it at the Wescon show in San Francisco in September 1975. It ran the Apple I and Apple II, the Commodore PET and VIC-20, the BBC Micro and, as variants, the Commodore 64, the Atari 2600 and the Nintendo Entertainment System. The Apple IIc beside it runs the 65C02, a low-power CMOS version of this chip.
facts: Launched at $25 in September 1975; MOS sold them from a jar at the Wescon show, and the price forced Motorola and Intel to cut theirs.
About 3,500 transistors on a die a few millimetres across, drawn by hand; the design clocked at 1 MHz.
Steve Wozniak chose it for the Apple I because it was the only processor he could afford.

artworks.title: Cray-1
artworks.medium: Electronic computer: ECL integrated circuits on hand-wired modules in a Freon-cooled C-shaped cabinet
artworks.description: The Cray-1 was the first supercomputer built by Seymour Cray's Cray Research and the fastest computer in the world from 1976 to 1982. Its C-shaped tower kept every wire short, and the padded bench around the base hid the power supplies, while liquid Freon carried away the heat of its hand-wired logic. Eighty or more were sold to weapons laboratories, weather centres and universities; this one stands at EPFL in Lausanne.
facts: The first Cray-1 was installed at Los Alamos National Laboratory in 1976, after being announced in 1975.
It ran at an 80 MHz clock (12.5 ns cycle) with 64-bit words and vector registers, and contained over 60 miles of wire, no piece longer than three feet.
Over 80 Cray-1s of all types were sold at $5–8 million each, making Seymour Cray a celebrity and Cray Research a success.

location.institution: National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution

artworks.medium: Single-board microcomputer: printed circuit board with integrated circuits

artworks.description: The Apple Computer 1 is an 8-bit personal computer designed by Steve Wozniak and sold from July 1976 by the newly founded Apple Computer Company, with Steve Jobs handling the business side. Unlike most hobbyist computers of its day it was delivered as a fully assembled and tested circuit board, built around a MOS 6502 processor; the buyer still had to add a power supply, keyboard, cassette recorder and television. The board shown here is an artist's reconstruction of a complete Apple I set-up, including the optional wooden case and Apple-1 Operation Manual.

Only about 175 to 200 boards were made before the Apple II replaced it; production ended on 30 September 1977.
Ran a MOS 6502 processor at 1 MHz with 4 KB of RAM (expandable to 8 KB) and displayed 40 x 24 characters on a television.

artworks.title: Apple II
artworks.medium: Personal computer: beige injection-moulded plastic case with integrated keyboard, printed circuit board with MOS 6502; monitor and floppy drives
artworks.description: The Apple II was Steve Wozniak's second machine and Apple's first product for the home: a complete computer in a plastic case with a keyboard, colour graphics on an ordinary television and expansion slots inside. Introduced in April 1977 and on sale from June at US$1,298, it made Apple a company and, with VisiCalc in 1979, made the personal computer a business tool. The set-up shown adds the Disk II floppy drives of 1978 and a monitor; this is an artist's model of the type, not a particular machine.

The eight expansion slots inside the case were insisted on by Wozniak over Steve Jobs's wish for two; they let the Apple II take a floppy controller in 1978.
VisiCalc, the first spreadsheet, ran only on the Apple II for its first year and sold many of the machines to businesses.
