artworks.title: A black hole
artworks.medium: Light traced through curved spacetime, computed live on the graphics processor
artworks.description:
What a black hole looks like, worked out before anyone had seen one. In 1979 Jean-Pierre Luminet, at the Paris Observatory at Meudon, traced rays of light backward from an observer's eye through the bent space around a black hole, on an IBM 7040 with punched cards, and plotted the result by hand with India ink, dot by dot. The picture surprised everyone: the far side of the glowing disc of gas around the hole is lifted into view above and below it, because light from behind bends over the top, and a thin ring of light rims the black shadow. Forty years later the Event Horizon Telescope's image of M87 showed the same ring.

What hangs here is not an image but the calculation itself, run afresh for every point of the window every frame as you move, so you can walk round it. The side of the disc coming toward you is brighter, as his was.
facts: Luminet's 1979 picture is the first scientific image of a black hole; it was computed, not observed.
Light from the far side of the disc reaches you over the top of the hole: that is why the ring seems to stand up behind it.
The film Interstellar's black hole of 2014 was made the same way, with Kip Thorne checking the equations.
The real thing, M87's black hole, was imaged in 2019 and hangs nearby.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/blackhole.ts: for every pixel of a square held up facing the visitor, a ray is traced back from the eye and bent through Schwarzschild spacetime around a mass at the square's centre, crossing a thin glowing disc; the method is Luminet's of 1979, done on the graphics chip. The stars behind are made up. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: The Mandelbrot set
artworks.medium: Fractal, computed live on the graphics processor
artworks.description:
Take a number c in the complex plane, start z at zero, and repeat z = z² + c. For some c the value stays bounded forever; for others it runs off to infinity. The set of c that stay is the black shape here, and its edge is infinitely detailed: zoom in anywhere on the boundary and new copies of the whole appear among seahorses, spirals and filaments, with no end to it. Benoit Mandelbrot made the first crude pictures at IBM on 1 March 1980, on a printer; Robert Brooks and Peter Matelski had drawn a rough one two years earlier.

Nothing here is a picture. The panel computes the set afresh every frame on the graphics chip as you watch, zooming slowly into the boundary and back out, as far as single-precision arithmetic allows.
facts: Every point of the boundary is a point where the behaviour of z changes from bounded to runaway; the boundary has dimension 2.
The set is connected, which Mandelbrot doubted from his pictures and Douady and Hubbard proved in 1982.
Along the real axis it contains the bifurcation cascade of the logistic map.
The zoom here stops at about eight thousand times; beyond that the GPU's arithmetic runs out of digits.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/mandelbrot.ts: a fragment shader iterates z squared plus c up to 300 times for every pixel every frame, zooming into the seahorse valley and back out over two minutes. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: Space Shuttle
artworks.medium: An artist's 3D model, at true size
artworks.description: The whole stack as it stood on the pad: the orbiter riding a tank of liquid hydrogen and oxygen the size of a grain silo, with two solid boosters strapped alongside that burned for two minutes and came down by parachute to be used again. Two million kilograms at lift-off, seven million pounds of thrust, and the first spacecraft to fly to orbit and land on a runway, 135 times from 1981 to 2011. It built the space station, carried Hubble up and fixed it five times, and lost two crews, Challenger in 1986 and Columbia in 2003. It stands here at its full 56 metres, off to the east; the orbiter Discovery, the real one, stands on the lane a little further on.
facts: The external tank was the only part thrown away each flight; it was painted white twice, then left orange to save 270 kg.
The main engines burned hydrogen at 3,300 degrees inside chambers cooled by the same hydrogen flowing through their walls.
Five orbiters flew: Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis and Endeavour; Enterprise flew only glide tests.
The programme cost about 200 billion dollars; a launch cost around 450 million.

Guinness World Records lists it as the best-selling desktop computer model of all time, with estimates of 12.5 to 17 million units sold.
Its MOS 6510 CPU, VIC-II video chip and SID 6581 sound chip were all made by Commodore's own chip subsidiary MOS Technology; production ended with Commodore's bankruptcy in April 1994.

The machine was usually sold with the matching 9-inch Monitor IIc shown here.

Weighs 7.5 lb (3.4 kg) and runs a 65C02 at 1.023 MHz with 128 KB of RAM.
First Apple product in the Snow White design language by Hartmut Esslinger of frog design; discontinued in August 1988 in favour of the IIc Plus.

artworks.title: Space Shuttle Discovery

location.name: Chantilly, Virginia
location.institution: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center

artworks.medium: Aluminium airframe under 24,000 silica heat-shield tiles and reinforced carbon-carbon leading edges
artworks.description: The most flown spacecraft there has ever been: thirty-nine missions between 1984 and 2011, a year of her life in orbit all told, 148 million miles. Discovery carried the Hubble Space Telescope up in 1990 and went back twice to service it, flew the first woman to pilot a shuttle, the first Russian cosmonaut on an American vehicle and John Glenn at seventy-seven, and was the ship chosen to return to flight after both the Challenger and Columbia losses. She is the Smithsonian's own scan, at true size, standing on her gear: 37 metres long, a 24 metre wingspan, 78 tonnes empty. Walk under the wing and look up at the tiles; each was fitted by hand and no two are alike.
facts: Thirty-nine flights, more than any other spacecraft; 5,830 orbits of the Earth.
Her last flight, STS-133 in March 2011, delivered a storage module and a humanoid robot to the International Space Station.
The black tiles on her underside shed the heat of re-entry, 1,650 °C, and are cool enough to hold a minute later.
She was flown to Washington on the back of a 747 in April 2012 and has been at the Udvar-Hazy Center since.

artworks.medium: Personal computer: beige plastic all-in-one case with built-in 9-inch monochrome display, separate keyboard and mouse
artworks.description: The Macintosh Plus of January 1986 is the first Macintosh in the original upright case to stay in production for years: the 1984 machine's 9-inch screen, mouse and windowed desktop, now with a megabyte of memory, a SCSI port and a keyboard with a numeric keypad. The Plus introduced the SCSI port to the Macintosh, which made fast external hard disks possible for the first time.
Its 512 by 342 pixel black-and-white screen is the same one the 1984 Macintosh used, in the same case; only the badge and keyboard give the model away.

artworks.title: International Space Station

creators.name: NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA and the Canadian Space Agency

date.label: crewed without a break since 2 November 2000

artworks.medium: NASA's 3D model, at true size
artworks.description: The largest thing people have built off the Earth: a football pitch of solar arrays and a truss the length of one, with pressurised modules strung along it that fifteen nations sent up piece by piece over thirteen years, beginning with a Russian module in November 1998 and an American one a fortnight later. It has been lived in without a break since 2 November 2000; some 280 people from 23 countries have been aboard, and it circles the Earth sixteen times a day at 28,000 kilometres an hour, 400 kilometres up, bright enough to be the third-brightest thing in the night sky when it passes over. It was built by two countries that had spent fifty years aiming missiles at each other. It hangs here to the west of the lane, at true size, as high as it is wide; walk out under it.
facts: Mass 420 tonnes; pressurised volume about that of a six-bedroom house.
The crew see sixteen sunrises a day. Experiments aboard have covered fire in weightlessness, protein crystals, and what a year in orbit does to a human body.
Forty-two assembly flights: thirty-seven by the Space Shuttle, five by Russian rockets.
NASA plans to bring it down into the Pacific in 2031.

Combining a phone, an iPod and an internet browser in one slab of aluminium and glass, it set the pattern that nearly every smartphone has followed since. artworks.title: Two black holes become one

creators.name: LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration

artworks.medium: Two black holes merging, computed live; the detectors' recording at the moment of merger
artworks.description:
At 09:50:45 on the morning of 14 September 2015, two detectors four thousand kilometres apart, in Louisiana and in Washington State, each four kilometres long, flexed by a fraction of the width of a proton, seven milliseconds apart. The signal rose in pitch and strength for a fifth of a second and stopped: two black holes, of thirty-six and twenty-nine times the mass of the sun, 1.3 billion light-years away, had spiralled together and merged, turning three suns' worth of mass into a ripple in the shape of space. Einstein had predicted such waves in 1916 and thought them too faint ever to detect.

What you see is the event run again, not a film of it, slowed a hundred times: the masses circling faster and closer, the sheet of space dented and rippling, the strain drawn as the detectors drew it, and at the merger, LIGO's recording of the chirp. The event is catalogued as GW150914, for the date.
facts: The detection came four days after the upgraded detectors switched on, before their official observing run began.
The waves' speed and the time difference between the two sites fix where in the sky they came from, roughly: the southern hemisphere.
Three solar masses of energy left as gravitational waves; for a tenth of a second the merger outshone all the stars in the observable universe combined.
Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the 2017 Nobel Prize for it.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/merger.ts: two masses inspiral on the leading-order chirp, slowed a hundredfold, denting a sheet that ripples with their quadrupole wave; a panel draws the strain, and at the merger LIGO's own recording of GW150914, pitched into hearing, is played (chirp.mp3 served beside the record, from the Gravitational Wave Open Science Center, CC BY 4.0). The program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: Falcon 9

date.label: first landing of an orbital booster, 21 December 2015

artworks.medium: An artist's 3D model, at true size
artworks.description: On the evening of 21 December 2015 a Falcon 9 put eleven satellites into orbit and then its first stage, 42 metres of it, turned round, flew back to Cape Canaveral, and set down upright on its legs on a concrete pad ten minutes after it had left. Rockets had always been thrown away; from here on the expensive part came home. Nine kerosene engines, a body built by a company that was thirteen years old, and a landing, controlled by grid fins and a single engine relit three times, that engineers had called impossible for sixty years. Boosters have since flown more than twenty times each, and the cost of reaching orbit fell by more than half. It stands here at its full 70 metres, off to the east, on its legs as it landed.
facts: The first stage comes back at Mach 6 and slows itself with its own engines; the grid fins steer it like a dart.
By 2025 the Falcon 9 had flown more than 500 times, more than any other orbital rocket.
A booster first flew twice in March 2017; the record stands above twenty flights.
The fairing halves are caught at sea and reused too.

artworks.title: AlphaGo's rack
artworks.medium: Photograph of a server rack
artworks.description: One rack of the machine that played. The AlphaGo that beat Lee Sedol ran across Google's data centres on 1,920 processors and 280 graphics chips, and on a new kind of chip, the tensor processing unit, which Google had built in secret for exactly this sort of arithmetic and announced two months after the match. A later AlphaGo Zero needed only four of them. This is a retired rack, kept and labelled.
facts: The match version used 48 TPUs; the program had been trained on thirty million positions from human games and then on games against itself.
Lee Sedol took the one game in five by finding a move the machine had thought one in ten thousand.
DeepMind retired AlphaGo from competition in 2017 after beating the world number one, Ke Jie, three games to none.

artworks.title: AlphaGo, move 37
artworks.medium: A game of Go, replayed live; the record of the game
artworks.description:
Go had been the game computers could not play. It has more possible positions than there are atoms in the universe, and the strength of a move is a matter of shape and feel that the best players could not put into rules. In March 2016 in Seoul, DeepMind's AlphaGo, a program that had learnt from thirty million human positions and then from millions of games against itself, played Lee Sedol, eighteen times a world champion, for a million dollars. In the second game, at move 37, it put a black stone on the fifth line at P10, a shoulder hit that no professional would play: the commentators thought it was a mistake, Lee left the room for a quarter of an hour, and the program had reckoned the odds of a human choosing it at one in ten thousand. It won the game, and the match 4 to 1.

The board here is playing the game through as you watch, stone by stone with the captures, as the demonstration boards in the commentary rooms showed it, and pauses at the move.
facts: Lee Sedol said afterwards: "I thought AlphaGo was based on probability calculation and that it was merely a machine. But when I saw this move, I changed my mind. Surely, AlphaGo is creative."
Fan Hui, the European champion who had lost to AlphaGo in secret the autumn before, said of move 37: "It's not a human move. I've never seen a human play this move. So beautiful."
Lee won game 4 with a move of his own, the wedge at move 78, that AlphaGo had thought as unlikely as its own move 37.
The next year AlphaGo Zero learnt the game from nothing but the rules, in three days, and beat the version that played Lee 100 games to 0.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/go.ts: the record of game 2 of the Google DeepMind Challenge Match (Seoul, 10 March 2016), AlphaGo Black, Lee Sedol White, B+Resign after 211 moves, replayed on a demonstration board with captures, dwelling on move 37. The game record itself is a fact, not a work; the moves were checked against three SGF copies (A. E. Brouwer's go archive, DeepMind's commented SGF, Go Game Guru) and Wikipedia's diagrams. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: Lee Sedol
artworks.medium: Photograph
artworks.description: Lee Sedol, born 1983 on the island of Bigeumdo, a professional at twelve, eighteen times a world champion, and in March 2016 the man who sat down across from a machine for five games and a million dollars and lost four. Here he is ten weeks later, giving away what the match had paid him. He had said before the match that he would win five to nothing or four to one. He kept playing for three more years and retired in 2019, saying that with AI at the top there was an entity that could not be defeated.
facts: His game 4 win, with the wedge at move 78 that AlphaGo had rated one in ten thousand, is the last time a human beat a top Go program in an even game.
He turned professional at twelve, the fifth-youngest ever in Korea.
He donated the LG sponsorship money for the match to a welfare centre for the developmentally disabled, where this photograph was taken.

artworks.title: James Webb Space Telescope

creators.name: NASA, ESA and CSA; Northrop Grumman; the Space Telescope Science Institute

location.name: The second Lagrange point, 1.5 million km from Earth

artworks.medium: NASA's 3D model, at true size
artworks.description: A mirror six and a half metres across, eighteen gold-plated beryllium hexagons, folded to fit inside a rocket and opened in space over two weeks, standing on a sunshield the size of a tennis court that keeps it colder than minus 220 degrees so it can see in infrared: the heat-light of the first galaxies, stretched by the expansion of the universe past the reach of any eye or of Hubble. It was twenty-five years in the making and sits a million and a half kilometres away, where no one can go to fix it; 344 things had to deploy in order and every one did. Six months after launch it sent back the deepest picture of the universe ever taken, which hangs on the next row.
facts: The mirror's gold is 48 grams in all, a layer a few hundred atoms thick; gold reflects infrared best.
It sees in infrared because light from the first galaxies has been stretched more than tenfold on its way to us.
Launched on an Ariane 5 from French Guiana so precisely that the fuel saved doubled its expected life, to twenty years.
It has found galaxies from 300 million years after the big bang, earlier and brighter than the models predicted.

artworks.title: Webb's First Deep Field

creators.name: NASA, ESA, CSA and the Space Telescope Science Institute

artworks.medium: Composite of near-infrared exposures, 12.5 hours in all
artworks.description: The deepest picture of the universe anyone had taken, shown by the President of the United States on the evening of 11 July 2022, twelve and a half hours of infrared exposure on a patch of the southern sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length. Nearly everything in it is a galaxy. The cluster at the centre, SMACS 0723, is so massive that its gravity bends the space around it into a lens, smearing the galaxies behind into the arcs you can see curving round it, and bringing into view light that set out more than thirteen billion years ago, when the universe was a few hundred million years old. Hubble would have needed weeks for this. Stand close: the smallest red smudges are the oldest things ever photographed.
facts: The cluster is 4.6 billion light-years away; the lensed arcs behind it are from the universe's first billion years.
The six-pointed spikes belong to the few stars in the field, in our own galaxy; they come from the mirror's hexagons and struts.
Thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky one could cover with a grain of sand; the whole sky holds some twenty million such patches.
Released a day early at the White House, then with four more pictures on 12 July: the Carina nebula, Stephan's Quintet, the Southern Ring and the spectrum of an exoplanet.
